habitat: Singly in floodplains and moist grassland, often at sewage works or in cattle pens and feedlots.
summary: A locally common summer visitor. Yellow below and green-grey above, with various head patterns that Newman names but does not describe. Non-breeding birds, especially females and immatures, are much duller, with the yellow faint and restricted to the lower belly. The call is tsee-ip. Newman names no months. The Kemp paper name Yellow Wagtail and the code NB were left unchanged.

sources.title: Kemp A.C., Herholdt J.J., Whyte I. & Harrison J. (2001). Birds of the two largest national parks in South Africa: a method to generate estimates of population size for all species and assess their conservation ecology. S. Afr. J. Sci. 97: 393–403.

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^4=16 mature individuals (non-breeding visitor); paper interval half–double → 8–32.

sources.title: Kemp A.C., Herholdt J.J., Whyte I. & Harrison J. (2001). Birds of the two largest national parks in South Africa: a method to generate estimates of population size for all species and assess their conservation ecology. S. Afr. J. Sci. 97: 393–403.

head.pattern: Head pattern varies by race. Newman names Blue-headed, Yellow-headed, Grey-headed, Sykes’s and Black-headed forms and does not describe the patterns.

upperparts.pattern: Green-grey upperparts, including the rump. Olive-green rather than grey. Green-grey is not a colour token.

underparts.pattern: Much duller. Yellow is faint and restricted to the lower belly. Identification of non-breeding males and females is almost impossible.

research.note: Newman calls it a locally common summer visitor and names no months, so status is summer-migrant and monthsPresent is unset. The named head patterns are not described, which is why this needs review. Grey Wagtail is a comparison Newman names and is not in this list. Population figures and the Kemp code NB were left unchanged.
